Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: related GloVe embeddings of 4,496 first-hand reports of 21 psychedelic drugs to receptor affinity profiles using partial least squares regression (PLSR), and reported associations between specific receptors and experiential themes.
Because affinities vary only between drugs, every report of a drug carries the same profile.
I show algebraically that within-drug variation drops out of every crossproduct with the affinities.
The published loadings can be reproduced from the drug means alone ( ), so the analysis rests on 21 drugs, with a Kish effective sample size of about 11, rather than on 4,496 reports.
The model is near-saturated at the drug level.

The cross-validation, receptor subset selection and loading interpretation have not been assessed at the drug level, and the associations have not been tested against chance or for generalisation beyond the few heavily weighted drugs, within the sample or to new ones.
A reanalysis of published values shows that the first three components closely follow the DMT-MDMA contrast ( ), mean report length ( ) and the LSD-DMT contrast ( ).
The length component follows from summing word vectors.
I propose drug-level validation, permutation and resampling analyses that can be run on the existing data.
Code reproducing all numbers is publicly available.

I read with interest the article by Suresh et al. (2026), who embedded 4,496 firsthand reports of 21 psychedelic drugs in a 100-dimensional GloVe space and related them, by partial least squares regression (PLSR) with 19 latent components (LC1-LC19), to normalised affinities (npKi) at 19 receptors.

text.text: From the loadings they report associations such as 5-HT1A and 5-HT1B with 'Cognitive Disruption', H1 with 'Interdimensional Communication', and 5-HT7a and 5-HT1E with 'Visual Complexity'.
The authors discuss many limitations openly, and the druglevel differences in experience they describe, such as between MDMA and DMT, are of interest in their own right.

Although the article is presented as hypothesis-generating, its abstract states that the analysis "reveals novel associ-r ≥ 0.998 r = 0.93 r = 0.96 r = 0.97 ations", and its conclusions that receptors "are distinctly associated" with specific effects and that such mappings provide "an empirical scaffold for designing next-generation compounds".

Exploration is a legitimate first step, but identifying which variables contribute to an outcome is an inferential goal, and evaluating a model on new data a predictive one, each with its own standard of evidence (Bzdok and Ioannidis 2019), and the validation used for either must itself be unbiased.

If the data cannot separate receptor contributions from drug identity, that limitation is itself worth reporting.
The model is also close to saturated at the drug level.
After centring, the 21 drug means span at most 20 dimensions, and 19 components were fitted.
Regressing an unrelated response on 19 predictors across 21 observations already gives an expected in-sample of at the drug level.
The published report-level of 0.19 does not contradict this, because it is diluted by withindrug variance that cannot explain by construction.

Model selection raises a related concern.

According to the supplement (ESM3), receptor subsets were formed by thresholds on the number of drugs with non-zero affinity, each subset was scored by fivefold cross-validation, and the subset with the highest explained semantic variance (19 receptors) was retained.
The selection is not described as nested within the cross-validation.
If the reported 0.74 and 0.19 are the scores of the selected subset on the same folds, they are optimistically biased (Varma and Simon 2006), a form of circular analysis.
